# Whole-page reader prompt

You are considering installing a Mac utility you have not used before. The attached screenshots show one proposed public landing page at desktop and narrow-phone widths. Some long-page views are also supplied as ordered section crops so you can read the details. The supplied text is the same page's full copy. Illustration rows are made-up examples, not customer outcomes.

Use only these screenshots and words. Do not browse, read files, run commands, call tools or use account or project context. Do not assume the product has capabilities not shown. Do not try to please the author.

Answer:
1. In one sentence, what does the product do and who is it for?
2. What is confusing or contradictory, in the words or the visual objects? Quote exact text or identify the visual moment.
3. Which sections or lines would you skip, and why? Which facts feel repeated?
4. What information is missing before you could decide?
5. What would make you install it, and what would make you leave? Separate product/security tradeoffs from page-presentation problems.
6. Who actually sorts and archives the mail: you by dragging, the app after you start it, or a background process? Say what evidence on the page led you there.
7. Explain how you would undo a mistaken archive and what email data leaves the Mac. If it is unclear, say so rather than inventing an answer.
8. Rate the page from 1 (poor) to 5 (clear) on: job clarity, ease of following the story, usefulness of the visuals, finding safety/data/requirements/cost information, and readiness to make a decision. Explain each rating briefly.

Finish with the three most important presentation changes, in priority order. A product limitation can remain a valid reason not to install even if the page explains it well.

Before you install
Google sign-in.
Connect Gmail through Google in your browser. zero never sees your password. You may see an unverified-app warning because zero hasn’t completed Google’s app review.
Sorting data.
TypeSafe’s Jev model receives sender, subject, a preview of up to 160 characters, whether you sent the latest message and whether you’ve replied to that sender before, your rules and learned preferences. No zero server receives your email.
Privacy policy
.
Sorting cost.
Bring your own Jev key, billed by TypeSafe. See
TypeSafe pricing
. The app is free and open source under AGPL-3.0.
Optional drafts.
Claude Code, or another AI coding tool you already use, can draft replies using its account and billing. Its provider receives thread previews, sent-mail samples, writing preferences and saved profile context. Review before
Send reply
. Drafts never send automatically.
Installer.
zero is not notarized by Apple. The installer may add Homebrew, Python, Node and the Google Workspace CLI. It adds Claude Code if no supported coding tool is installed.
Choose what needs to stay.
Run zero from its menu bar to sort connected Gmail accounts. AI applies your rules. Starred mail stays untouched. Uncertain threads stay in your inbox. Check your first runs: the model can make mistakes.

Rules
## Keep a thread only if it genuinely needs me to act
- A real person is awaiting my reply or my decision.
- There is an unanswered direct question or request addressed to me.
- A payment has actually failed or is a live problem (not a routine receipt).
- It is a legal, contractual, or dispute matter.
- There is an explicit deadline with a real consequence.
## Archive everything else (reversibly)
- Cold outreach, sales, prospecting, pitches, even when the sender uses a real
human name and I have never replied to them.
- Receipts, invoices, statements, order and delivery confirmations.
- Notifications, alerts, digests, newsletters, social, marketing, surveys.
